about: Building types (roadmap BT1c1): farm buildings. Same fields as lineage.json.

types.name: Aisled barn

period.text: developed in the 12th and 13th centuries; the oldest standing, the Barley Barn at Cressing Temple, c. 1220; still built in the 18th century in parts of southern England (Hambrook, c. 1771), the last year not known

types.structure: timber frame in which posts and braces divide a central space from side aisles

sources.title: Tithe barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The medieval aisled barn was developed in the 12th and 13th centuries, following the examples of royal halls, hospitals and market halls.

sources.title: Cressing Temple
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Barley Barn (English Heritage listing 1123865) is an early thirteenth century (c. 1220) barn modified in later centuries, and is the oldest standing timber-framed barn in the world.

sources.title: Aisled Barn from Hambrook
sources.author: Weald & Downland Living Museum
sources.quote: During the repair of the barn the date 1771 was found scratched on an original rafter.

sources.title: Aisled Barn from Hambrook
sources.author: Weald & Downland Living Museum
sources.quote: Built in the mid-18th century, the barn is of a type common in West Sussex and eastern Hampshire.

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: AISLED BARN
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A barn in which a central space is separated from side aisles by posts and braces.

period.text: an Old English word; the oldest standing c. 1220 (Cressing Temple); built ever since, now usually of steel

sources.title: Cressing Temple
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Barley Barn (English Heritage listing 1123865) is an early thirteenth century (c. 1220) barn modified in later centuries, and is the oldest standing timber-framed barn in the world.

sources.title: Barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Modern barns are more typically steel buildings.

types.name: Tithe barn (great medieval barn)

period.text: the great aisled barns from the 12th and 13th centuries (c. 1200); about 200 medieval ones (to 1550) survive in Britain; later barns are also called tithe barns; tithes in kind ended with the Tithe Act 1836

types.note: English Heritage: not one of England's surviving architecturally impressive barns was a tithe barn; many were monastic barns.

sources.title: Tithe barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: not one of England's surviving architecturally impressive barns was a tithe barn, although such barns existed

sources.title: Tithe barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many were monastic barns, originally used by the monastery itself or by a monastic grange.

sources.title: Tithe barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The medieval aisled barn was developed in the 12th and 13th centuries, following the examples of royal halls, hospitals and market halls.

sources.title: Tithe barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The total number of surviving medieval barns (dated up to 1550) in Britain may be estimated about 200.

sources.title: Tithe barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: There are many extant barns that date from after the Medieval period and may be called "tithe barns" by their owners or councils.

sources.title: Tithe Commutation Act 1836
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It replaced the ancient system of payment of tithes in kind with monetary payments.

types.name: Threshing barn

period.text: the design little changed from the 12th century to the 19th; after the 1880s many were turned into cow houses; no source gives the last one built (c. 1880 here)

types.plan: a central threshing floor between large double doors and a smaller door opposite, with the crop stored on either side

sources.title: Barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The design of these typically remained unchanged between the 12th and 19th centuries.

sources.title: Barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Many barns were converted into cow houses and fodder processing and storage buildings after the 1880s.

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: THRESHING BARN
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A barn usually containing a single, central threshing floor.

sources.title: Barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Characterised by large double doors in the centre of one side, a smaller one on the other, and storage for cereal harvest or unprocessed on either side.

types.name: Cruck barn

period.text: the oldest tree-ring dated crucks from about the mid-13th century; used later where curved timber was to hand; revived in green-oak framing since about 1980

types.structure: pairs of curved timbers (blades, often one oak split in two) forming an A-frame that carries the roof independently of the walls

sources.title: Cruck
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The oldest surviving crucks with dates confirmed by tree ring analysis date from around the middle of the 13th century.

sources.title: Cruck
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Where naturally curved timbers were convenient and available, carpenters continued to use them at much later dates.

sources.title: Cruck
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: During the current revival of green-oak framing for new building work, which has occurred mainly since approximately 1980 in the UK, genuine cruck frames have quite often been included in traditionally carpentered structures.

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: CRUCK BARN
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A barn in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.

sources.title: Cruck
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The crucks or cruck "blades" are a single oak tree riven (split) in two to form an equally shaped A frame.

types.name: Bank barn

period.text: Cumbria by the 1660s; most built 1750-1860; the last just before the First World War

types.plan: two storeys built into a slope: a threshing barn above, entered from the upper side, and animal housing below

sources.title: Bank barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The great majority of bank barns were built in Cumbria between 1750 and 1860, and the last were built just before World War I.

sources.title: Bank barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The bank barn had made its first appearance in Cumbria by the 1660s on the farms of wealthy farmers

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: BANK BARN
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A multi-purpose, two-storey barn, built on a hillside with entrances at both levels to a first floor threshing barn and ground floor animal housing.

types.name: Hay barn (Dutch barn)

period.text: from the end of the 18th century; most from the 19th century; still very common, now mostly for straw, and easily put up and taken down

types.structure: a roof on posts or poles with open sides, for ventilation

sources.title: Dutch barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Hay barns came into use at the end of the 18th century.

sources.title: Dutch barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These are a relatively recent development in the history of British farm architecture, most examples dating from the 19th century.

sources.title: Dutch barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Dutch barns are still very common in the U.K., and are nowadays most commonly used to store straw rather than hay.

sources.title: Dutch barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Due to their ease of construction these structures are often considered temporary and appear and disappear in the landscape

sources.title: Dutch barn
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: They have a roof, but no walls.

sources.title: FISH Thesaurus of Monument Types: HAY BARN
sources.author: Historic England
sources.quote: A special type of barn, lacking a threshing floor, usually with open walls, intended for the dry and well ventilated storage of hay only.

types.name: Gin gang (horse engine house)

period.text: from Meikle's threshing machine (c. 1786); most built c. 1785-1851, the peak 1800-1830; the portable horse engine (c. 1840) ended most building, but the last were built in the Isle of Wight and Cornwall until 1868

types.plan: a one-storey round, polygonal or square house against the threshing barn, the drive passing through the wall

sources.title: Threshing machine
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The first threshing machine was invented circa 1786 by the Scottish engineer Andrew Meikle

sources.title: Gin gang
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The truly portable horse engine was invented around 1840; this obviated the necessity for building further gin gangs.

sources.title: Gin gang
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Most gin gangs were built from around 1785 to 1851, peaking in 1800 to 1830.

sources.title: Gin gang
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The most recent ones were built in the Isle of Wight and Cornwall from 1845 to 1868.

sources.title: Gin gang
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: a structure built to enclose a horse engine, usually circular but sometimes square or octagonal, attached to a threshing barn

sources.title: Gin gang
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It was almost always of one storey and it could be circular, polygonal or square.

sources.title: Gin gang
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: There was a hole for a drive−shaft or drive−belt, linking it with the threshing barn.

types.name: Oast house

period.text: after hops came to England in the mid-16th century; first described in 1574; the earliest surviving at Golford, Cranbrook (the article dates it to the 17th century in one place and 1750 in another); built as late as 1950, and a large modern one in 1982

types.structure: kilns with thin perforated drying floors over a fire, the heat leaving through a cowl in the roof
types.plan: a rectangular one- or two-storey stowage with one or more kilns

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: It dates from some time in the 17th century and closely mirrors the first documentary evidence on oasts soon after the introduction of hops into England in the mid-16th century.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest description of an oast dates from 1574.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest surviving purpose-built oast is at Golford, Cranbrook, built in 1750.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Oasts were built as late as 1948 (Upper Fowle Hall, Paddock Wood), or 1950 (Hook Green, Lamberhurst).

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: These vast buildings can process hops from several farms, as at Norton near Teynham in Kent, built in 1982.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The drying floors were thin and perforated to permit the heat to pass through and escape through a cowl in the roof which turned with the wind.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: An oast house consists of a rectangular one- or two-storey building (the "stowage") and one or more kilns

types.name: Dovecote (doocot)

period.text: from the 12th century; the earliest surely dated free-standing one in England 1326 (Garway); Scottish doocots built well into the 18th century, then no longer needed; a 20th-century revival by pigeon fanciers

types.plan: early ones round (beehive), tapering to a domed roof with an opening at the top; in Scotland from the late 16th century rectangular lecterns with a mono-pitched roof

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest surviving, definitely dated free-standing dovecote in England was built in 1326 at Garway in Herefordshire.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest known examples of dove-keeping occur in Norman castles of the 12th century

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Doocots were built well into the 18th century in increasingly decorative forms, then the need for them died out though some continued to be incorporated into farm buildings as ornamental features.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: However, the 20th century saw a revival of doocot construction by pigeon fanciers

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Early purpose-built doocots in Scotland are often of a "beehive" shape, circular in plan and tapering up to a domed roof with a circular opening at the top.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: In the late 16th century, they were superseded by the "lectern" type, rectangular with a mono-pitched roof sloping fairly steeply in a suitable direction.

period.text: Roman: pigeon keeping a passion in Rome by Caesar's conquest of Gaul (from 58 BC); pigeon holes at Caerwent suggest the Romans brought them to Britain; none known in Britain after Roman rule ended in 410

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Pigeon keeping was then a passion in Rome: the Roman-style, generally round, columbarium had its interior covered with a white coating of marble powder.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The presence of dovecotes is not documented in France before the Roman invasion of Gaul by Caesar.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The Romans may have introduced dovecotes or columbaria to Britain since pigeon holes have been found in Roman ruins at Caerwent.

sources.title: Roman Britain
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The occupation lasted from 43 AD to 410 AD.

types.name: Laithe house

types.plan: house and barn under one roof, with no cross passage and no way through between them

sources.quote: Some were housed in a specially constructed building, a gin gang, which would be attached to a threshing barn.

links.claim: The first oast houses were adapted barns; by the 18th century tall kilns with conical roofs had been developed for the draught, square at first, round from about 1800.

sources.title: Oast house
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: Early oast houses were simply adapted barns, but by the 18th century the distinctive tall buildings with conical roofs had been developed to increase the draught.

sources.title: Oast house

sources.quote: At first, these were square, but around 1800 roundel kilns were developed in the belief that they were more efficient.

links.claim: Dove-keeping in England is first known from nest-holes in Norman castle keeps of the 12th century (Rochester); the free-standing dovecote follows (the earliest surely dated, 1326). The sources give the order, not the descent.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest known examples of dove-keeping occur in Norman castles of the 12th century (for example, at Rochester Castle, Kent, where nest-holes can be seen in the keep), and documentary references also begin in the 12th century.

sources.title: Dovecote
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The earliest surviving, definitely dated free-standing dovecote in England was built in 1326 at Garway in Herefordshire.

links.claim: The Romans may have brought dovecotes to Britain (pigeon holes at Caerwent), but doves are thought not to have been commonly kept until after the Norman Conquest.

sources.title: Dovecote

views: Roman introduction: pigeon holes in the Roman ruins at Caerwent.
